lead: Unit 1 builds the transistor model that every later CMOS circuit sits on: how a MOS capacitor forms a channel, when the transistor is cutoff, linear or saturated, what the current equations are, and where the simple model breaks. After this unit you can pick the operating region of any nMOS or pMOS from its terminal voltages, compute ID, VT, capacitance and leakage, and explain why short channels and FinFETs forced the textbook model to change.
about: The unit starts at the silicon surface. Chapter 1.1 takes the MOS capacitor through accumulation, depletion and inversion, then turns inversion into the cutoff, linear and saturation regions of nMOS and pMOS devices. Chapter 1.2 puts a number on the onset of inversion, the threshold voltage, and shows how the body voltage shifts it. Chapter 1.3 writes the square-law I-V equations and the transconductance. Chapter 1.4 adds what the square law misses: mobility degradation, velocity saturation and channel length modulation. Chapter 1.5 collects the capacitances and parasitic resistances that later set delay. Chapter 1.6 covers scaling and short-channel effects, 1.7 covers leakage and subthreshold conduction, and 1.8 ends with FinFETs, a topic only a few universities teach.

chapters.idea: A MOS capacitor becomes a transistor when the gate voltage inverts the surface, and the three operating regions are simply three shapes of that inversion channel.
chapters.depth: Cross-section of the MOS capacitor: gate, oxide of thickness tox, body doped NA. Define flat-band voltage, then the three states as the gate voltage rises: accumulation (majority holes pile at the surface), depletion (a depletion region of width Wd opens under the oxide), inversion (minority electrons form a conducting channel once the surface potential reaches 2φF). Move to the four-terminal nMOS with source, drain, gate and body, and state that a channel exists only while VGS > VT. Give the region table for both nMOS and pMOS: cutoff, linear (some syllabi say triode or ohmic), saturation, with the pinch-off boundary at VDS = VGS − VT. Keep the algebra out; only the region tests are needed here.

figure.title: Choosing the nMOS region
figure.aria: A decision chart that names the nMOS region from the terminal voltages: cutoff when the gate voltage is below the threshold, otherwise linear when the drain voltage is below the overdrive, otherwise saturation.

chapters.example: An nMOS has VT = 0.5 V, kn′ = 100 µA/V² and W/L = 10, so kn′(W/L) = 1000 µA/V². (a) With VGS = 1.5 V and VDS = 0.4 V the overdrive VGS − VT = 1.0 V, and 0.4 V < 1.0 V, so the device is linear: ID = kn′(W/L)[(VGS − VT)VDS − VDS²/2] = 1000 µA/V² × (1.0 × 0.4 − 0.08) V² = 320 µA. (b) Hold VGS at 1.5 V and raise VDS to 1.5 V: now VDS > 1.0 V, so the device saturates and ID = ½ × 1000 µA/V² × (1.0 V)² = 500 µA.
chapters.trap: Swapping the nMOS and pMOS tests. A pMOS conducts when VGS is more negative than −|VT|, so compare |VGS| with |VT| and |VDS| with |VGS| − |VT|, and remember VDS is negative when the source is the higher-potential terminal. Also, the VDS in the region test is the full drain-to-source voltage, not the excess above the overdrive.
chapters.prereq: School-level electrostatics and a first semiconductor devices course: doping, the pn junction and the idea of a depletion region.
chapters.leave: The closed-form threshold expression to 1.2, the current equations and their derivation to 1.3, and the capacitances to 1.5.

chapters.idea: Threshold voltage is the part of the gate voltage spent on band bending and depletion charge before inversion charge appears, and it grows when the source rises above the body.
chapters.depth: Build VT from its parts: flat-band voltage VFB (gate-to-body work function difference plus fixed oxide charge), the 2φF band-bending term, and the depletion charge term √(2qεsiNA·2φF)/Cox, giving VT0 = VFB + 2φF + √(2qεsiNA·2φF)/Cox with Cox = εox/tox. Define φF = (kT/q) ln(NA/ni). Body effect: VT = VT0 + γ(√(2φF + VSB) − √(2φF)), with γ = √(2qεsiNA)/Cox in units of √V. Explain the mechanism: a reverse body-source bias adds charge to the depletion region, so the gate must work harder before inverting the surface. Give typical γ values (0.1 to 0.5 √V) and note VT falls by roughly 1 to 2 mV per °C as temperature rises. In one line, name the SPICE Level-1 parameters that carry these numbers: VTO, GAMMA, PHI, TOX.

figure.aria: Two curves of threshold voltage against source-to-body voltage starting from 0.45 V, the stronger body-effect coefficient giving the steeper rise.

chapters.trap: Writing VBS where the formula needs VSB. That flips the sign and makes the threshold appear to fall when the body is reverse biased. γ is not dimensionless; its unit is √V, so an answer in volts is wrong. And the body effect is zero when the source is tied to the body, which is why it matters for stacked transistors and not for the ones sitting on the rails.
chapters.leave: Threshold roll-off and drain-induced barrier lowering to 1.6; what a low VT costs in leakage to 1.7.

chapters.idea: The square-law equations give drain current from the overdrive voltage and the W/L ratio, with a quadratic saturation branch.
chapters.depth: Sketch the derivation: channel charge per unit area Q(x) = Cox(VGS − VT − V(x)), drift velocity set by the lateral field, integrate from source to drain. Results for the nMOS: linear ID = kn′(W/L)[(VGS − VT)VDS − VDS²/2] for VDS < VGS − VT; saturation ID = ½ kn′(W/L)(VGS − VT)² for VDS ≥ VGS − VT. Define kn′ = µnCox and kp′ = µpCox, with µp roughly 0.25 to 0.5 times µn. Show the transfer characteristic ID against VGS and the output family ID against VDS for several VGS. Give the small-signal transconductance in saturation, gm = kn′(W/L)(VGS − VT), and the on-resistance in the linear region near VDS = 0, Ron ≈ 1/[kn′(W/L)(VGS − VT)]. Write the pMOS versions with all signs flipped. Note that some syllabi call this the square-law, Shichman-Hodges or SPICE Level-1 model.

figure.aria: Output characteristics of a square-law nMOS with 1 mA/V² gain and 0.5 V threshold, each curve rising linearly then flattening at the saturation current for its gate overdrive.

chapters.example: An nMOS has kn′ = 100 µA/V², W/L = 20, VT = 0.5 V, VGS = 1.5 V and VDS = 2 V. The overdrive is 1.0 V and VDS is larger, so the device is saturated: ID = ½ × 100 µA/V² × 20 × (1.0 V)² = 1 mA. Its transconductance is gm = 100 µA/V² × 20 × 1.0 V = 2 mA/V. The same device in the linear region at VDS = 0.5 V carries ID = 2000 µA/V² × (1.0 × 0.5 − 0.125) V² = 0.75 mA.
chapters.trap: Putting VDS into the saturation formula in place of the overdrive (VGS − VT), which makes the current keep growing after saturation. Dropping the factor ½, which doubles every saturation answer. And writing W/L where the formula needs L/W, which is easy to do when rearranging for a given current.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 for the regions and 1.2 for VT.
chapters.leave: λ, mobility degradation and velocity saturation to 1.4; the capacitances that must charge these currents to 1.5.

chapters.idea: The square law assumes low field and a long channel; mobility degradation, velocity saturation and channel length modulation are the three corrections that take the model to a real device.
chapters.depth: Mobility degradation: the vertical gate field pulls carriers against the rough oxide interface, so µeff ≈ µ0/(1 + θ(VGS − VT)), which flattens the transfer curve at high VGS. Velocity saturation: the drift velocity vd = µE/(1 + E/Ec) levels off at vsat, about 10⁷ cm/s for electrons in silicon; when the lateral field reaches Ec = vsat/µ, the saturation current becomes roughly ID ≈ vsatCoxW(VGS − VT), linear in overdrive, and gm stops growing with overdrive. Define the knee VDSsat = (VGS − VT)EcL/((VGS − VT) + EcL). Channel length modulation: the pinch-off point moves toward the source as VDS rises, the effective channel shortens to L − ΔL, so ID = ½kn′(W/L)(VGS − VT)²(1 + λVDS) with λ roughly proportional to 1/L; the output resistance is ro = 1/(λID). Say that these three, together with the threshold shifts of 1.6, are what syllabi list as non-ideal I-V effects or second-order effects.

figure.title: From square law to a measured curve
figure.aria: A chain of four corrections applied one after another to the square-law current, ending at the measured output characteristic with its finite slope.

chapters.example: An nMOS has W = 1 µm, L = 0.25 µm, Cox = 8.6 fF/µm², µn = 500 cm²/V·s, vsat = 10⁷ cm/s and VGS − VT = 2 V. Square law: ½µnCox(W/L)(VGS − VT)² = ½ × 0.05 m²/V·s × 8.6e-3 F/m² × 4 × 4 V² = 3.44 mA. The critical field is Ec = vsat/µn = 10⁵ / 0.05 = 2 × 10⁶ V/m, so EcL = 2e6 × 0.25e-6 = 0.5 V and VDSsat = (2 × 0.5)/(2 + 0.5) = 0.4 V. The velocity-saturated current is vsatCoxW(VGS − VT − VDSsat) = 10⁵ × 8.6e-3 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.6 = 1.38 mA, so the square law over-predicts by about 2.5 times. With λ = 0.1 V⁻¹ the output resistance is ro = 1/(0.1 × 1.38e-3 A) = 7.2 kΩ.
chapters.trap: Applying the (1 + λVDS) factor in the linear region, where the channel is not pinched off. Treating mobility degradation and velocity saturation as one effect: one comes from the vertical gate field and the other from the horizontal drain field, and only velocity saturation changes the saturation current from quadratic to linear in overdrive.
chapters.leave: DIBL, punch-through and hot carriers to 1.6; gate tunnelling and GIDL to 1.7.

chapters.idea: Every pair of MOSFET terminals is a capacitor that the driving gate charges and discharges each cycle, and series resistances slow that charging.
chapters.depth: Oxide capacitance per unit area Cox = εox/tox and total gate area capacitance CoxWL. The split among terminals depends on the region (Meyer model): in cutoff the channel is absent, so only overlap capacitances Cgs = CGSO·W and Cgd = CGDO·W remain; in saturation Cgs ≈ ⅔CoxWL plus overlap while Cgd is overlap only; in linear the channel behaves as a resistor and the channel capacitance splits evenly, Cgs = Cgd ≈ ½CoxWL plus overlap. Overlap capacitance comes from lateral diffusion of source and drain under the gate; SPICE carries CGSO, CGDO and CGBO per unit width. Junction capacitances Csb and Cdb each have an area part (CJ × area) and a sidewall part (CJSW × perimeter), both voltage dependent: Cj = Cj0/(1 + V/VB)^m with m about 0.3 to 0.5. Parasitic resistances: source and drain sheet resistance, silicide contact resistance, and the distributed polysilicon gate resistance, modelled as an RC ladder for a wide device.

figure.title: Gate capacitance by region, columns Cgs, Cgd, Cgb
figure.aria: A three-row table giving gate-source, gate-drain and gate-bulk capacitance in cutoff, linear and saturation, with the bulk taking the full oxide capacitance only in cutoff and the source taking most of it in saturation.

chapters.example: An nMOS has W = 1 µm, L = 0.25 µm, tox = 4 nm and an overlap of 0.02 µm at each side. Cox = 3.45e-11 / 4e-9 = 8.6 fF/µm², so the gate area capacitance is 8.6 × 1 × 0.25 = 2.15 fF and the overlap per side is 8.6 × 1 × 0.02 = 0.17 fF. In saturation Cgs = ⅔ × 2.15 + 0.17 = 1.43 + 0.17 = 1.60 fF and Cgd = 0.17 fF, giving a total gate capacitance of about 1.77 fF. The same device in cutoff presents only 0.17 fF from gate to source and gate to drain.
chapters.trap: Using CoxWL as the gate capacitance in every region; in saturation only about two-thirds of the channel charge is reached from the source. Ignoring overlap capacitance, which becomes the dominant part once L is short. And writing the junction capacitance as a fixed number when it depends on the voltage across the junction.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 for the channel, 1.2 for the region boundary at VT.
chapters.leave: Propagation delay and the RC delay model to Unit 3; extraction of real parasitics from layout to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Scaling shrinks L, tox and VDD together so the field pattern is preserved, but below about a quarter micrometre the gate loses control of the channel and a family of short-channel effects appears.
chapters.depth: Constant-field scaling (some syllabi call it Dennard scaling) by a factor S > 1: W, L, tox, VDD and VT divide by S, doping NA multiplies by S, Cox multiplies by S. Then capacitance scales 1/S, current 1/S, delay 1/S, power per gate 1/S² and power density stays at 1. Contrast constant-voltage scaling, where VDD is fixed and power density rises as S. Short-channel effects: threshold roll-off as L falls, drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL, VT shifting with VDS so the output curve gains extra slope), punch-through when the source and drain depletion regions meet, hot carriers (electrons near the drain gaining enough energy to enter the oxide), lightly doped drain (LDD) structures that spread the peak field, negative bias temperature instability (NBTI, a slow shift of pMOS VT under gate stress at temperature), and time-dependent oxide breakdown. Keep formula use light; the scaling table and the effect list are what is examined.

figure.title: Constant-field scaling by factor S
figure.aria: A scaling table showing that in constant-field scaling lengths, oxide thickness and supply voltage divide by S, doping multiplies by S, and power per gate falls as 1 over S squared while power density is unchanged.

chapters.example: A gate has C = 10 fF, runs at VDD = 2.5 V and 100 MHz, so its dynamic power is CVDD²f = 10e-15 F × 6.25 V² × 1e8 Hz = 6.25 µW. Scale the process by S = 2 with constant field: C becomes 5 fF, VDD becomes 1.25 V, and because delay halves the clock doubles to 200 MHz. New power = 5e-15 × 1.5625 × 2e8 = 1.56 µW, which is 6.25/4, so power per gate falls by S² and the power per unit area is unchanged.
chapters.trap: Mixing constant-field and constant-voltage scaling when asked about power density; only the constant-field case keeps it flat. And confusing DIBL with punch-through: DIBL is a drain-field shift of VT, punch-through is the source and drain depletion regions merging so the gate no longer controls the current at all.
chapters.prereq: 1.3 for the current equations and 1.4 for the field-dependent effects.
chapters.leave: Leakage numbers to 1.7; the multi-gate answer to 1.8; process steps and layout rules to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Below threshold the MOSFET still conducts, exponentially in VGS, and that subthreshold current plus gate and junction leakage is now a large share of chip power.
chapters.depth: Subthreshold conduction for VGS < VT: the channel is weakly inverted and ID ≈ µCox(W/L)(n − 1)VT² e^((VGS − VT)/(nVT)) (1 − e^(−VDS/VT)), where VT in the exponent is the thermal voltage kT/q ≈ 26 mV at 300 K and n = 1 + Cd/Cox lies between 1.0 and 1.5. Flag the clash of symbols: Vth or VT0 for threshold, VT for kT/q. Subthreshold swing S = 2.3nVT = 2.3VT(1 + Cd/Cox), typically 70 to 100 mV per decade, with a hard floor of 60 mV/decade at room temperature. Off current Ioff is quoted per µm of width at VGS = 0 and VDS = VDD. Temperature dependence: Ioff roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise. Geometry dependence: shorter L and narrower W shift VT and so change Ioff, which is why leakage is quoted per µm. Other leakage paths: direct gate oxide tunnelling (serious below about 2 nm of oxide), gate-induced drain leakage (GIDL, band-to-band tunnelling in the drain overlap at low VGS), and reverse-biased junction leakage.

figure.aria: Two straight-line subthreshold plots of log drain current against gate voltage, the steeper 60 mV per decade line reaching a given current at a much lower gate voltage.

chapters.example: A process has subthreshold swing S = 80 mV/decade and Ioff = 10 nA/µm at VT = 0.3 V. Raising the threshold by 100 mV cuts leakage by 10^(100/80) = 10^1.25 = 17.8, so Ioff falls to 0.56 nA/µm. A chip carrying 10 mm of total transistor width therefore leaks 5.6 µA instead of 100 µA. The swing also gives n: from S = 2.3nVT, n = 0.080 V / (2.3 × 0.026 V) = 1.34.
chapters.trap: Using the same symbol VT for threshold voltage and thermal voltage; state clearly which one the exponent uses. Claiming a swing below 60 mV/decade for a bulk MOSFET at room temperature, which is physically impossible. And saying the transistor is off at VGS = 0 when Ioff is what the datasheet actually reports.
chapters.prereq: 1.2 for VT and its temperature trend, 1.3 for the above-threshold current the subthreshold curve joins.
chapters.leave: Power budgeting and sleep-mode design to Unit 3; leakage test structures to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: When a planar gate can no longer control a short channel, lifting the channel into a thin fin and wrapping the gate around it restores control, so leakage falls without a thinner oxide.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it to structure, effective width and one comparison. Start from the reason: a planar gate controls the channel from one side only, so scaling L demands thinner oxide and heavier doping, and leakage climbs anyway. Fin structure: a silicon fin of width Wfin and height Hfin with the gate covering three sides (tri-gate) or two (double gate). Effective width per fin Weff = 2Hfin + Wfin; the fin body is fully depleted, so the channel is undoped or lightly doped. Width quantisation: drive strength is set by the number of fins, not by drawing any width you like. Threshold is set by gate work function and fin width rather than body doping. Gate-all-around nanosheet devices extend the same idea to four sides. One short comparison of planar against FinFET on control, leakage, layout and cost.

figure.title: Gate control from one side to four
figure.aria: A progression from a planar gate through a thin fully depleted body to a fin with the gate on three sides and then a gate wrapped all the way around the channel.

chapters.example: A FinFET has Wfin = 10 nm and Hfin = 30 nm. The effective width per fin is 2Hfin + Wfin = 2 × 30 + 10 = 70 nm. A cell that needs 700 nm of drive width therefore uses 10 fins. If the process delivers 1 mA per µm of effective width, one fin carries 70 nm × 1 mA/µm = 70 µA and ten fins carry 0.7 mA.
chapters.trap: Using Wfin alone as the effective width, which under-counts the drive current by a factor of about seven in this example. Forgetting width quantisation, so a request for 700 nm of width must round to a whole number of fins. And claiming the FinFET removes short-channel effects; it reduces them.
chapters.prereq: 1.6 for short-channel effects and 1.7 for the leakage they cause.
chapters.leave: Fin patterning and process flow to Unit 2; fin-based cell layout and design rules to Unit 2; variability and testing to Unit 6.
